newsitem.title: JORDAN: Israel president urges Arafat to agree Hebron deal.
newsitem.headline: Israel president urges Arafat to agree Hebron deal.

text.p: Israeli President Ezer Weizman urged Palestinian Authority President Yasser Arafat on Wednesday to work harder to break a deadlock over Israel's long-delayed troop redeployment in the West Bank town of Hebron.
Weizman, speaking in Amman after talks with Jordan's King Hussein, said further stalling in the talks could threaten the whole peace process.

"I call on my neighbour Abu Ammar (Arafat) to try and move things a bit differently," Weizman told a news conference. "I know he has certain opinions, but I'm sure the Khalil (Hebron) thing could be solved quicker if there was a little more willingness to do so."
He said a national security alert in Israel this week had shown once again how vulnerable peace talks remained.

"If anything happens, (any) terror activity in Israel, this would affect negatively, enormously, the process," he said. "Therefore the speed that we conclude the deal on Khalil is of prime importance."

Weizman's visit, the first to Jordan by an Israeli president, was intended to repair ties after a row over Moslem holy sites in Jerusalem and the eight-month-overdue Hebron redeployment agreed by Israel's previous Labour government.

"Even if there were no tension, I would have come," said the president, whose largely ceremonial role has not stopped him trying to improve relations with Arabs since the election in May of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who opposes trading captured Arab land for peace.
But Weizman played down any hopes of instant return to the warm ties following the 1994 Israeli-Jordan peace treaty, when Jordan was seen as Israel's closest Arab peace partner.
"We are going to be in touch. I can't tell you whether (the tension) is easing now. I hope it will ease," he said.

Netanyahu angered Jordan in September when he opened a tunnel entrance near Moslem sites in Jerusalem without consulting King Hussein, whose "special role" in supervising the sites was recognised in the 1994 agreement.

The tunnel opening sparked widespread violence in the West Bank and Gaza Strip in which 75 people were killed and prompted dark warnings from King Hussein of a return to violent confrontation if Netanyahu reneged on accords signed by previous governments, including the Hebron deal.
On Wednesday the king was more optimistic.
"There are still those who are maybe opposed to peace...but the overwhelming majority have opted for peace and we hope it will be reflected more and more by everyone," he said.
Few Jordanians, who gained little of the promised peace dividend from the Jordan-Israeli treaty, are enthusiastic supporters of the deal.
Officials say Israel has also failed to implement much of the accord, particularly over cooperation on scarce water resources and opening up Palestinian and Israeli markets to Jordanian goods.
"Two years ago...there were perhaps more hopes," Weizman said. "But our national anthem says we haven't lost hope... (though) I don't expect anyone else to adopt this anthem."
